transitivity: both — transitive (cook dinner), intransitive (the rice is cooking)
gloss: To prepare food using heat.
examples: I *cook* dinner for the family most nights.
She *cooked* the whole meal in under an hour.
The beans have been *cooking* since noon.

transitivity: both — transitive (bake a cake), intransitive (the bread is baking)
gloss: To cook food in an oven with dry heat, especially bread, cakes, or cookies.
examples: I *bake* bread every Sunday morning.
She *baked* two pies for the party.
The cookies are *baking* right now.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: bake → baking, never bakeing.

transitivity: both — transitive (boil an egg), intransitive (the water is boiling)
gloss: To heat a liquid until it bubbles, or to cook food in bubbling water.
examples: *Boil* the potatoes for twenty minutes.
I *boiled* the water for tea.
The soup has been *boiling* far too long.

ru: тушить на слабом огне, кипеть на медленном огне
transitivity: both — transitive (simmer the sauce), intransitive (the pot is simmering)
gloss: To cook something gently in liquid just below boiling.
examples: Let the sauce *simmer* for an hour.
She *simmered* the stock all afternoon.
The chili has been *simmering* since breakfast.

transitivity: both — transitive (fry an egg), intransitive (the bacon is frying)
gloss: To cook food in hot oil or fat.
examples: I usually *fry* the onions first.
He *fried* two eggs for breakfast.
Something is *frying* in the kitchen.
contrast: Consonant + -y becomes -ies and -ied: fries, fried — but -ing keeps the y: frying.

transitivity: both — transitive (roast a chicken), intransitive (the potatoes are roasting)
gloss: To cook meat or vegetables with dry heat in an oven or over a fire.
examples: We *roast* a turkey every Thanksgiving.
I *roasted* the carrots with olive oil and salt.
The chicken has been *roasting* for an hour.

ru: жарить на гриле, пожарить на углях
transitivity: both — transitive (grill a steak), intransitive (we grilled out back)
gloss: To cook food on a metal grate over fire or hot coals.
examples: Dad likes to *grill* burgers in the backyard.
We *grilled* corn and chicken on Saturday.
The steaks are *grilling* now.

gloss: To cook food with strong heat coming from directly above it in an oven.
examples: *Broil* the fish for about four minutes.
I *broiled* the cheese until it bubbled.
She has already *broiled* the tops of the peppers.
contrast: American English: broil = cook under the oven's top element. The British call that grilling.

transitivity: both — transitive (steam the rice), intransitive (the dumplings are steaming)
gloss: To cook food over boiling water using the hot vapor.
examples: *Steam* the broccoli for five minutes.
I *steamed* the dumplings instead of frying them.
The rice is *steaming* in a covered pot.

gloss: To cook eggs or fish gently in barely simmering liquid.
examples: He *poaches* an egg every morning.
I *poached* the salmon in white wine.
She has never *poached* an egg before.
contrast: Verbs ending in -ch take -es in the third person: poach → poaches.

gloss: To cook meat slowly in a covered pot with a little liquid.
examples: *Braise* the short ribs for three hours.
We *braised* the lamb in red wine.
The beef has been *braising* all afternoon.

gloss: To fry food quickly in a little hot fat, stirring or tossing it.
examples: *Sauté* the mushrooms until they turn golden.
I *sautéed* the garlic for about thirty seconds.
He is *sautéing* onions for the sauce.
contrast: The accent stays in every form: sautés, sautéed, sautéing.

ru: обжаривать на сильном огне, подрумянивать до корочки
gloss: To brown the surface of meat quickly over very high heat.
examples: *Sear* the steak hard on both sides.
She *seared* the scallops in a smoking pan.
The chef has already *seared* the roast.

transitivity: both — transitive (toast the bread), intransitive (the bagel is toasting)
gloss: To brown bread, nuts, or spices with dry heat.
examples: I *toast* the walnuts before adding them.
He *toasted* four slices of rye.
The bagel is *toasting* right now.

gloss: To heat or cook food in a microwave oven.
examples: Just *microwave* the leftovers for two minutes.
I *microwaved* the soup and burned my tongue.
She is *microwaving* a frozen dinner.

gloss: To heat an oven to the right temperature before the food goes in.
examples: *Preheat* the oven to 350 degrees.
I *preheated* the oven an hour ago and then forgot about it.
The oven is still *preheating*.

transitivity: both — transitive (reheat the pizza), intransitive (the casserole reheats well)
gloss: To heat cooked food again after it has cooled.
examples: Don't *reheat* rice twice.
I *reheated* the pizza in a skillet.
The stew has been *reheated* so many times that it fell apart.

transitivity: both — transitive (heat the oil), intransitive (the pan is heating)
gloss: To make something warm or hot.
examples: *Heat* the oil until it shimmers.
She *heated* the milk on the stove.
The skillet is *heating* on the back burner.

transitivity: both — transitive (warm the plates), intransitive (the soup is warming)
gloss: To make food or drink moderately hot, or to become moderately hot.
examples: *Warm* the plates before you serve.
I *warmed* the bread in the oven.
The cider is *warming* on the stove.

ru: жарить на барбекю, готовить на углях
transitivity: both — transitive (barbecue ribs), intransitive (they barbecue every weekend)
gloss: To cook food slowly outdoors over smoke or hot coals.
examples: They *barbecue* every Fourth of July.
We *barbecued* ribs all afternoon.
He is *barbecuing* chicken in the backyard.
contrast: Spelled barbecue (short form BBQ); barbeque is nonstandard. The -e drops before -ing: barbecuing.

transitivity: both — transitive (brown the beef), intransitive (the crust is browning)
gloss: To cook the surface of food until it turns brown.
examples: *Brown* the beef before you add the tomatoes.
I *browned* the butter until it smelled nutty.
The crust is *browning* nicely.

transitivity: both — transitive (caramelize the sugar), intransitive (the onions caramelized)
gloss: To cook sugar, or the sugar in a food, until it turns brown and sweet.
examples: Slow heat will *caramelize* the onions.
She *caramelized* the sugar for the flan.
The shallots have *caramelized* beautifully.
contrast: American English spells it -ize; British English uses caramelise.

gloss: To boil vegetables briefly and then drop them into cold water.
examples: *Blanch* the green beans for two minutes.
I *blanched* the tomatoes to loosen their skins.
The spinach has already been *blanched*.
contrast: Third person adds -es: blanch → blanches.

transitivity: both — transitive (overcook the pasta), intransitive (salmon overcooks quickly)
gloss: To cook food too long, so that it turns dry or mushy.
examples: Don't *overcook* the pasta.
I *overcooked* the salmon again.
The eggs were badly *overcooked*.

ru: поливать соком или жиром при жарке
gloss: To spoon juices or melted fat over food while it roasts.
examples: *Baste* the turkey every half hour.
He *basted* the chicken with herb butter.
She has been *basting* the roast all morning.

gloss: To make a hissing sound, the way food does in hot fat.
examples: The onions *sizzle* the moment they hit the pan.
The bacon *sizzled* and spat at me.
Steaks were *sizzling* on the grill.

gloss: To cut food into pieces with quick strokes of a knife.
examples: *Chop* the parsley very fine.
I *chopped* an onion and cried the whole time.
He is *chopping* vegetables for the stew.
contrast: One vowel + one final consonant doubles: chop → chopped, chopping.

gloss: To cut something into thin flat pieces.
examples: *Slice* the bread thick.
She *sliced* the tomatoes for the sandwiches.
I cut my finger *slicing* an apple.
contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: slicing, not sliceing.

gloss: To cut food into small even cubes.
examples: *Dice* the potatoes into half-inch cubes.
I *diced* the celery and the carrots.
He is *dicing* onions for the soup.

gloss: To chop food into very small pieces.
examples: *Mince* two cloves of garlic.
She *minced* the ginger with a heavy knife.
The shallots have already been *minced*.

gloss: To rub food against a rough metal surface to make small shreds.
examples: *Grate* the cheese over the pasta.
I *grated* a whole block of cheddar.
She is *grating* carrots for the salad.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *great*.

transitivity: both — transitive (peel a potato), intransitive (my sunburn is peeling)
gloss: To take the skin off a fruit or vegetable.
examples: *Peel* the apples before you slice them.
I *peeled* five pounds of potatoes.
She is *peeling* shrimp at the sink.

gloss: To cut away unwanted parts of food, such as fat or stems.
examples: *Trim* the fat off the steak.
I *trimmed* the ends of the green beans.
The butcher has already *trimmed* the roast.
contrast: Double the m: trim → trimmed, trimming.

gloss: To press something hard until it breaks into small pieces.
examples: *Crush* the garlic with the flat of the knife.
I *crushed* the crackers for the topping.
She is *crushing* ice for the drinks.

transitivity: both — transitive (crumble the cheese), intransitive (the cookie crumbled)
gloss: To break into small crumbs, or to break something into crumbs.
examples: *Crumble* the feta over the salad.
I *crumbled* the bacon into the batter.
The dry cake *crumbled* the moment I cut it.

gloss: To crush cooked food into a soft mass.
examples: *Mash* the potatoes with warm milk.
He *mashed* a banana for the baby.
The avocado has already been *mashed*.

transitivity: both — transitive (squeeze a lemon), intransitive (squeeze past the counter)
gloss: To press something firmly, often to get liquid out of it.
examples: *Squeeze* half a lemon over the fish.
She *squeezed* the juice from four oranges.
He is *squeezing* the water out of the spinach.

transitivity: both — transitive (crack an egg), intransitive (the bowl cracked)
gloss: To break the shell of an egg or a nut, or to split with a sharp sound.
examples: *Crack* three eggs into the bowl.
I *cracked* the walnuts with a hammer.
The mixing bowl has *cracked* down one side.

gloss: To beat eggs together and cook them in a pan while stirring.
examples: I'll *scramble* a couple of eggs.
He *scrambled* six eggs for the three of us.
She is *scrambling* eggs with cheese and chives.

ru: снимать пену или жир с поверхности, снять
gloss: To lift fat or foam off the top of a liquid.
examples: *Skim* the foam off the stock.
I *skimmed* the fat from the gravy.
The cook has been *skimming* the broth for an hour.
contrast: Double the m: skim → skimmed, skimming.

gloss: To pass flour or sugar through a fine mesh to remove the lumps.
examples: *Sift* the flour and the baking powder together.
I *sifted* powdered sugar over the cake.
The dry ingredients have all been *sifted*.

gloss: To pour a liquid through a sieve to separate out the solids.
examples: *Strain* the sauce before serving.
She *strained* the broth through cheesecloth.
I am *straining* the pasta now.

ru: сливать воду, откидывать на дуршлаг, слить
transitivity: both — transitive (drain the pasta), intransitive (let the fries drain)
gloss: To let liquid run off food or out of a container.
examples: *Drain* the pasta but save a cup of the water.
I *drained* the beans and rinsed them twice.
The fries are *draining* on a paper towel.

gloss: To wash something quickly with clean water.
examples: *Rinse* the rice until the water runs clear.
He *rinsed* the berries in a colander.
The lettuce has been *rinsed* twice already.

transitivity: both — transitive (wash the greens), intransitive (this pan washes easily)
gloss: To clean something with water.
examples: *Wash* the vegetables before you cook them.
I *washed* the dishes right after dinner.
He is *washing* lettuce at the sink.
contrast: Third person adds -es: wash → washes.

transitivity: both — transitive (soak the beans), intransitive (the pan is soaking)
gloss: To leave something in liquid for a long time.
examples: *Soak* the beans overnight.
I *soaked* the raisins in rum.
The roasting pan is *soaking* in the sink.

transitivity: both — transitive (dissolve the yeast), intransitive (the sugar dissolved)
gloss: To mix a solid into a liquid until it disappears.
examples: *Dissolve* the yeast in warm water.
The sugar *dissolved* in seconds.
The salt has completely *dissolved*.
contrast: Two s's, and they are pronounced /z/: di-ZAHLV.

transitivity: both — transitive (stir the soup), intransitive (stir constantly)
gloss: To move a spoon around in food or liquid to mix it.
examples: *Stir* the sauce so it doesn't stick.
She *stirred* sugar into her coffee.
I have been *stirring* this risotto for twenty minutes.
contrast: Double the r: stir → stirred, stirring.

transitivity: both — transitive (mix the batter), intransitive (oil and water don't mix)
gloss: To combine two or more things so that they become one.
examples: *Mix* the flour and the salt in a big bowl.
He *mixed* the batter by hand.
The dough is *mixing* in the machine.
contrast: Third person adds -es: mix → mixes.

gloss: To put two or more ingredients together.
examples: *Combine* the wet and the dry ingredients.
I *combined* the two sauces into one.
Once the eggs have been *combined* with the sugar, add the flour.

gloss: To beat eggs, cream, or sauce quickly with a wire tool.
examples: *Whisk* the eggs until they turn pale.
She *whisked* the dressing together in a jar.
He is *whisking* the sauce to keep it smooth.

gloss: To beat cream or egg whites until they hold air and stiffen.
examples: *Whip* the cream until soft peaks form.
I *whipped* the egg whites for the meringue.
The cream has been *whipped* too long and turned to butter.
contrast: Double the p: whip → whipped, whipping.

gloss: To mix a light ingredient into a heavier one with gentle turning strokes.
examples: Gently *fold* the egg whites into the batter.
She *folded* the berries into the dough.
The whipped cream is being *folded* in now.
contrast: In recipes it takes *into*: fold the egg whites **into** the batter.

gloss: To press and fold dough with your hands until it is smooth.
examples: *Knead* the dough for about ten minutes.
I *kneaded* the bread while the oven heated.
She has been *kneading* dough since dawn.
contrast: Silent k, and it sounds exactly like *need*.

transitivity: both — transitive (swirl the pan), intransitive (cream swirled through the coffee)
gloss: To move a liquid around in a circle, or to move that way.
examples: *Swirl* the pan to coat it with butter.
He *swirled* the wine in his glass.
Cream was *swirling* through the black coffee.

transitivity: both — transitive (thicken the gravy), intransitive (the sauce thickened)
gloss: To make a liquid thicker, or to become thicker.
examples: A spoonful of flour will *thicken* the gravy.
The sauce *thickened* as it cooled.
The stew has *thickened* nicely.

transitivity: both — transitive (soften the butter), intransitive (let it soften)
gloss: To make something soft, or to become soft.
examples: Let the butter *soften* on the counter.
I *softened* the onions in oil first.
The raisins have *softened* in the hot water.
contrast: The t is silent: SAW-fun, not SOFT-un.

gloss: To add salt, pepper, or other flavorings to food.
examples: *Season* the soup at the very end.
She *seasoned* the chicken with paprika and garlic.
The meat has been *seasoned* and is resting.
contrast: Season something **with** salt — never 'by salt'.

gloss: To give food or drink a particular taste.
examples: One bay leaf will *flavor* the whole pot.
They *flavored* the syrup with vanilla.
This oil is *flavored* with chili and garlic.
contrast: American flavor; British flavour. Same split in savor / savour.

gloss: To add salt to food.
examples: *Salt* the water before the pasta goes in.
I *salted* the eggplant to draw out the water.
The broth has already been *salted*.
contrast: The l is pronounced: SAWLT.

transitivity: both — transitive (marinate the beef), intransitive (let it marinate)
gloss: To soak food in a seasoned liquid before cooking it.
examples: *Marinate* the chicken for at least an hour.
We *marinated* the steak overnight.
The tofu has been *marinating* since morning.

gloss: To preserve food in vinegar or salt water.
examples: My grandmother *pickles* cucumbers every August.
We *pickled* a dozen jars of beets.
These onions have been *pickled* in red wine vinegar.

gloss: To preserve meat or fish with salt, smoke, or drying.
examples: They *cure* the ham for eighteen months.
He *cured* the bacon himself.
The salmon is still *curing* in salt and sugar.

gloss: To flavor and preserve food by hanging it in smoke.
examples: They *smoke* their own brisket out back.
We *smoked* the ribs for six hours.
The trout has been *smoked* over applewood.

gloss: To make food or drink sweeter.
examples: *Sweeten* the tea with honey.
She *sweetened* the berries with a little sugar.
The lemonade has already been *sweetened*.

gloss: To scatter small amounts of something over a surface.
examples: *Sprinkle* salt over the fries.
He *sprinkled* cinnamon on the oatmeal.
She is *sprinkling* powdered sugar on the donuts.
contrast: Either sprinkle salt **on/over** the dish, or sprinkle the dish **with** salt.

gloss: To pour a thin stream of liquid slowly over food.
examples: *Drizzle* olive oil over the salad.
She *drizzled* honey on the yogurt.
Chocolate had been *drizzled* across the whole plate.

gloss: To cover food with a thin layer of something.
examples: *Coat* the fish in flour before frying it.
I *coated* the pan with butter.
The chicken has been *coated* in breadcrumbs.
contrast: Coat it **in** or **with** something, never 'coat by'.

gloss: To spread a liquid over food with a brush.
examples: *Brush* the dough with beaten egg.
He *brushed* the ribs with sauce every few minutes.
She is *brushing* melted butter over the rolls.
contrast: Third person adds -es: brush → brushes.

gloss: To press a seasoning firmly onto the surface of food.
examples: *Rub* the spices into the meat.
I *rubbed* a cut garlic clove on the toast.
The roast has been *rubbed* with salt and pepper.
contrast: Double the b: rub → rubbed, rubbing.

gloss: To spread butter or oil on a pan so that food will not stick.
examples: *Grease* the pan before you pour in the batter.
I *greased* two cake tins.
The baking sheet has already been *greased*.

gloss: To spread butter on something.
examples: *Butter* both sides of the bread.
She *buttered* the toast while it was still hot.
He is *buttering* a whole stack of rolls.

gloss: To coat food with a shiny liquid such as syrup or thin icing.
examples: *Glaze* the ham with brown sugar and mustard.
She *glazed* the donuts while they were warm.
The carrots have been *glazed* in butter and honey.

gloss: To spread a thick sweet icing over a cake.
examples: Let the cake cool before you *frost* it.
She *frosted* the cupcakes with buttercream.
The layer cake has been *frosted* and decorated.
contrast: Americans frost a cake; the British ice it. The sweet topping itself is frosting.

gloss: To make something look attractive by adding things to it.
examples: The kids *decorate* the cookies every December.
She *decorated* the cake with fresh berries.
They are *decorating* gingerbread houses at the table.

gloss: To add a small decorative food to a finished dish.
examples: *Garnish* the soup with chives.
He *garnished* each plate with a lemon wedge.
The cocktails were *garnished* with mint.
contrast: A false friend: English garnish is a decoration, not Russian гарнир — that is a **side** or **side dish**.

gloss: To fill food with a mixture before cooking it.
examples: *Stuff* the peppers with rice and beef.
We *stuffed* the turkey on Thanksgiving morning.
The shells have been *stuffed* with ricotta.
contrast: Stuff something **with** a filling.

gloss: To arrange food in flat layers, one on top of another.
examples: *Layer* the noodles, the sauce, and the cheese.
She *layered* the potatoes in a buttered dish.
I am *layering* the trifle now.

transitivity: both — transitive (roll the dough), intransitive (the meatball rolled off the plate)
gloss: To flatten dough with a rolling pin, or to wrap food into a tube shape.
examples: *Roll* the dough into a thin circle.
He *rolled* the sushi very tightly.
The pastry has been *rolled* and chilled.
contrast: Homophone of *role*.

transitivity: both — transitive (pour the batter), intransitive (the syrup pours slowly)
gloss: To make a liquid flow out of a container.
examples: *Pour* the batter into the pan.
She *poured* two glasses of milk.
He is *pouring* the sauce over the pasta.
contrast: Sounds like *pore*. You pour something **into** or **over** a thing.

transitivity: both — transitive (fill the pot), intransitive (the kettle fills fast)
gloss: To make something full.
examples: *Fill* the pot with cold water.
I *filled* six jars with jam.
The kitchen was *filled* with the smell of bread.
contrast: Fill something **with** a thing — never 'fill by'.

gloss: To put something on the top of a dish.
examples: *Top* each bowl with sour cream.
She *topped* the pie with whipped cream.
The pizza is *topped* with fresh basil.
contrast: Double the p: top → topped, topping. It takes **with**.

transitivity: both — transitive (flip the pancake), intransitive (the burger flipped onto the coals)
gloss: To turn food over quickly so the other side cooks.
examples: *Flip* the pancakes when bubbles appear.
He *flipped* the burgers exactly once.
She is *flipping* an omelet in the pan.
contrast: Double the p: flip → flipped, flipping.

transitivity: both — transitive (chill the dough), intransitive (let the pie chill)
gloss: To make food or drink cold, usually in a refrigerator.
examples: *Chill* the dough for an hour before rolling it.
I *chilled* the wine before dinner.
The pie has been *chilling* since noon.

gloss: To keep food cold in a refrigerator.
examples: *Refrigerate* the leftovers right away.
I *refrigerated* the dough overnight.
Opened jars must be *refrigerated*.

transitivity: both — transitive (defrost the chicken), intransitive (the turkey is defrosting)
gloss: To let frozen food become unfrozen.
examples: *Defrost* the chicken in the refrigerator, not on the counter.
I *defrosted* the shrimp under cold water.
The turkey is still *defrosting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (thaw the berries), intransitive (the beef thawed)
gloss: To become unfrozen, or to make something unfrozen.
examples: Let the berries *thaw* before you use them.
The ground beef *thawed* in about an hour.
The pie crust has *thawed* enough to unroll.

gloss: To treat food so that it keeps for a long time.
examples: Salt and vinegar *preserve* vegetables.
She *preserved* twenty pounds of peaches.
These lemons have been *preserved* in salt.

transitivity: both — transitive (seal the bag), intransitive (the lids sealed overnight)
gloss: To close something tightly so that air cannot get in.
examples: *Seal* the bag before you freeze it.
I *sealed* the jars while they were still hot.
All the lids have *sealed* properly.

gloss: To keep food somewhere until it is needed.
examples: *Store* the flour in an airtight container.
We *stored* the apples in the basement.
The cookies are being *stored* in the freezer.

transitivity: both — transitive (cool the syrup), intransitive (let the bread cool)
gloss: To become less hot, or to make something less hot.
examples: Let the bread *cool* on a rack.
The soup *cooled* faster than I expected.
The cake has *cooled* enough to frost.

transitivity: both — transitive (reduce the wine by half), intransitive (let the sauce reduce)
gloss: To boil a liquid until part of it evaporates and the flavor concentrates.
examples: *Reduce* the wine by half.
I *reduced* the sauce until it coated the spoon.
The stock has been *reducing* for an hour.
contrast: General American drops the y-sound: ri-DOOS, not ri-DYOOS.

ru: пробовать на вкус, попробовать; иметь вкус
transitivity: both — transitive (taste the sauce), intransitive (it tastes salty)
gloss: To try a small amount of food, or to have a particular flavor.
examples: *Taste* it before you add more salt.
I *tasted* the sauce and reached for the pepper.
This soup has always *tasted* better the next day.
contrast: Say 'it tastes good', not 'it tastes well'. Compare flavors with **like**: it tastes like lemon.

transitivity: both — transitive (serve the fish), intransitive (they serve until ten)
gloss: To give food or drink to someone at a meal.
examples: *Serve* the fish with rice and lemon.
They *served* dinner at eight sharp.
This soup is usually *served* cold.

transitivity: both — transitive (chew your food), intransitive (chew slowly)
gloss: To break food up with your teeth.
examples: *Chew* your food properly.
The steak was so tough that I *chewed* it forever.
He is still *chewing* the last bite.

transitivity: both — transitive (swallow a pill), intransitive (it hurts to swallow)
gloss: To make food or drink go down your throat.
examples: *Swallow* the pill with plenty of water.
She *swallowed* the last of her coffee and stood up.
I have *swallowed* something the wrong way.

transitivity: both — transitive (sip your tea), intransitive (sip slowly)
gloss: To drink a very small amount at a time.
examples: *Sip* it slowly — it's boiling hot.
He *sipped* his coffee and said nothing.
She was *sipping* tea by the window.
contrast: Double the p: sip → sipped, sipping.

transitivity: both — transitive (gulp your milk), intransitive (he gulped and nodded)
gloss: To swallow a large amount of liquid quickly.
examples: Don't *gulp* your milk like that.
He *gulped* half the bottle in one breath.
She was *gulping* water after the run.

transitivity: both — transitive (nibble a cracker), intransitive (nibble on chips)
gloss: To eat something in small bites.
examples: The kids *nibble* on crackers all afternoon.
She *nibbled* one corner of the cookie.
Mice have been *nibbling* at the bread.
contrast: Usually nibble **on** or **at** something.

transitivity: both — transitive (munch popcorn), intransitive (munch on chips)
gloss: To eat something noisily and steadily.
examples: They *munch* popcorn through the whole movie.
He *munched* an apple on the way to work.
She is *munching* on carrot sticks.
contrast: Third person adds -es: munch → munches. Often munch **on** something.

gloss: To eat small amounts of food between meals.
examples: I *snack* far too much when I study.
We *snacked* on chips and salsa before dinner.
He has been *snacking* all afternoon.
contrast: Takes no object: you snack **on** something.

gloss: To eat dinner, especially in a formal place or a restaurant.
examples: They *dine* out every Friday.
We *dined* at a little place near the river.
The room where the family had *dined* was still set.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: dining, not dineing — hence dining room.

gloss: To eat a large, rich meal with great pleasure.
examples: Every November we *feast* for two solid days.
They *feasted* on crab and sweet corn.
We had *feasted* so well that nobody moved.
contrast: Feast **on** something.

gloss: To eat something quickly and hungrily.
examples: Teenagers *devour* whatever is in the fridge.
He *devoured* three slices in under a minute.
The whole cake had been *devoured* by noon.

gloss: To enjoy the taste of something slowly and fully.
examples: *Savor* the first bite.
She *savored* every spoonful of the soup.
He is *savoring* his last cup of decent coffee.
contrast: American savor; British savour.

gloss: To want a particular food very strongly.
examples: I *crave* salty things in the winter.
She *craved* pickles all through the pregnancy.
He has been *craving* his mother's soup for months.

ru: голодать, умирать от голода; морить голодом
transitivity: both — transitive (starve the animals), intransitive (the village starved)
gloss: To suffer or die from a lack of food.
examples: No one should *starve* in a country this rich.
Thousands *starved* through that winter.
I'm *starving* — when is dinner?
contrast: 'I'm starving' is everyday exaggeration for 'I'm very hungry'.

transitivity: both — transitive (order a pizza), intransitive (have you ordered yet?)
gloss: To ask for food or drink in a restaurant or from a store.
examples: I always *order* the same thing here.
We *ordered* two pizzas and a salad.
He is *ordering* takeout for everyone.

gloss: To try a small amount of food or drink in order to judge it.
examples: You can *sample* three cheeses for free.
We *sampled* every pie at the county fair.
She is *sampling* the new menu tonight.

transitivity: both — transitive (measure the flour), intransitive (the pan measures ten inches)
gloss: To find or take an exact amount of something.
examples: *Measure* the flour — don't guess.
I *measured* out two cups of sugar.
She is *measuring* the vanilla very carefully.

transitivity: both — transitive (weigh the flour), intransitive (it weighs two pounds)
gloss: To find out how heavy something is, or to have a certain weight.
examples: *Weigh* the dough before you divide it.
The butcher *weighed* the roast for me.
The flour has been *weighed* and set aside.
contrast: Silent gh, and it sounds exactly like *way*.

gloss: To make food ready to be cooked or eaten.
examples: I *prepare* the vegetables the night before.
She *prepared* a three-course meal by herself.
Dinner is being *prepared* right now.

transitivity: both — transitive (ferment the cabbage), intransitive (the dough fermented)
gloss: To change sugar into alcohol or acid through the action of yeast or bacteria.
examples: Let the dough *ferment* overnight.
The cabbage *fermented* for three weeks.
The wine has been *fermenting* since October.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, fur-MENT; the noun is FUR-ment.

transitivity: both — transitive (brew coffee), intransitive (the tea is brewing)
gloss: To make coffee, tea, or beer.
examples: I *brew* a pot of coffee every morning.
He *brewed* his own beer for years.
The tea is still *brewing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (steep the tea), intransitive (let it steep)
gloss: To leave tea or herbs in hot liquid so that the flavor comes out.
examples: *Steep* the tea for four minutes.
I *steeped* the mint in hot water.
The leaves have been *steeping* too long.

transitivity: both — transitive (stew the lamb), intransitive (the beef is stewing)
gloss: To cook meat or fruit slowly in liquid in a covered pot.
examples: *Stew* the lamb with onions and carrots.
She *stewed* apples for the pie filling.
The beef has been *stewing* for three hours.
contrast: General American drops the y-sound: STOO, not STYOO.

gloss: To dip food quickly into a liquid.
examples: *Dunk* the cookie in your milk.
He *dunked* the bread in the olive oil.
She is *dunking* fries into her milkshake.
contrast: Dunk something **in** or **into** a liquid.

transitivity: both — transitive (slurp the noodles), intransitive (don't slurp)
gloss: To eat or drink with a loud sucking noise.
examples: In Japan it is fine to *slurp* noodles.
He *slurped* his soup and his sister glared.
Someone was *slurping* the last of the milkshake.

transitivity: both — transitive (a paper bag ripens pears), intransitive (the fruit ripened)
gloss: To become ripe and ready to eat, or to make fruit ripe.
examples: Tomatoes *ripen* fast on a sunny windowsill.
The avocados *ripened* in a paper bag.
The peaches have all *ripened* at once.

transitivity: both — transitive (cater a wedding), intransitive (they cater for big parties)
gloss: To provide and serve the food for an event.
examples: They *cater* weddings all summer long.
A local deli *catered* the whole reception.
She has been *catering* corporate lunches for ten years.
contrast: Americans cater an event; the British cater **for** it. Cater **to** someone means to give them just what they want.
